transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 45 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Lin (Redwood AE), Carlos Romero (Redwood SE), Alex Chen (Greenline CTO), Priya Kapoor (Greenline ML Eng), Jordan Blake (Greenline VP Eng)
---
Summary: quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics. Covered streaming responses, request parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop), retry/backoff strategies, and demoed a simple streaming chat in the Console and a curl/SDK example. Customer concerned about latency (real-time chat), cost per token, and safe retry behavior on 5xx/timeouts. Next steps: pricing, SDK snippets, POC dataset + benchmark window.
---
Topics: streaming vs polling, tokenization/cost, retries & idempotency, rate limits, params tuning, console demo, sample payloads
---
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a 30-40 minute walkthrough of Redwood's hosted API for chat and text generation focusing on streaming, how to tune params, and retry best practices. Carlos will show the demo.
[00:12] Alex: thanks Maya, excited to see latency stuff; we'll be integrating into our customer support chat so sub 300ms would be ideal but we know that's aggressive.
[00:20] Carlos: got it, we'll call out realistic expectations. quick intro: Redwood hosted API offers a simple REST endpoint and SDKs, streaming via server-sent events / chunked responses, and a Console where you can prototype.
[00:35] Priya: quick question on data retention — do you keep logs? we need SOC2-level controls.
[00:40] Maya: yes, default is ephemeral but for enterprise tenants we offer options and PII redaction, plus SOC 2 + audit logs; we can share the security whitepaper after the call.
[01:05] Carlos: demo plan: first show Console streaming example, then show a curl and Node SDK example, and finish with tuning params and retry/backoff guidance.
[02:15] [Console share sound] Carlos: ok switching to the Console. here's a chat example — prompt on the left, model selection up top. Note: model catalog shows latencies and token pricing estimates for each model variant.
[03:02] Carlos: I'm going to start a streaming request. you'll see partial tokens arrive as SSE chunks. this is helpful for UI responsiveness — you can render progressively.
[03:20] Alex: does streaming cost the same as non-streaming?
[03:25] Carlos: yes cost is per token generated regardless of streaming. small overhead on request count but tokens are main cost.
[04:05] [00:04:05] Carlos: here's the example payload: temperature=0.2, top_p=0.95, max_tokens=256, stop sequences set to ['\nUSER:'] for our demo. If you need deterministic output keep temp near 0.
[04:40] Priya: we often need to produce structured JSON. do you recommend any settings?
[04:48] Carlos: yes — few things: 1) use lower temperature, consider logit bias for known tokens, 2) use stop sequences or function-calling / structured output support if available, 3) validate and fallback on parse errors client-side. we'll show an example.
[05:30] [05:30] Carlos: starting a curl streaming example — curl -N -H 'Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY' -d '{"model":"rwd-small","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize..."}]}' https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat/stream
[06:05] Jordan: in the SDK do you expose reconnect helpers for stream disconnects?
[06:12] Carlos: good question. SDKs have helpers for reconnecting and resuming relatively simply. we recommend client-side buffering and idempotency keys for replay safety.
[06:50] Maya: quick notes on retries: generally for 429s implement exponential backoff with jitter; for 5xx transient errors retry a few times but avoid duplicating actions if the request had side effects. for pure generation it's usually safe to retry, but be mindful of duplication of downstream logging.
[07:25] Priya: how do you recommend we handle token accounting with retries? we don't want to overpay for repeated attempts.
[07:33] Carlos: server-side we only bill for tokens actually generated; if a retry generates the same tokens you'll pay for them. recommended pattern: do short timeouts, if you get a partial chunk you can resume from cache or detect duplicate by content hash. Redwood also supports prefix/KV caching in Dedicated but on hosted we offer some caching heuristics.
[08:15] Alex: can you talk about rate limits and burst behavior? our app has spiky traffic at peak hours.
[08:23] Maya: hosted plan has per-account rate limits with burst windows; we can increase on request, and Dedicated gives predictable throughput for heavy workloads.
[09:00] Carlos: back to streaming: in browsers SSE is easiest; in mobile you may use websockets or chunked HTTP. here's the sample Node snippet: const stream = client.chat.stream({model:'rwd-small', messages: []}); stream.on('data', chunk => {/* render */}); stream.on('end', ()=>{/* finalize */});
[09:40] Priya: any best practices for UI? we want to show partial thought vs final answer.
[09:46] Carlos: show partials as typing, buffer small tokens so you don't flicker, and commit when you see sentence-end punctuation or a special end-token. also expose a cancel button to abort extra tokens.
[10:30] [10:30] Carlos: demo: adjusting parameters — increasing temperature to 0.8 produces more creative responses; lowering top_p to 0.6 reduces tail risk. watch out: higher temperature can increase token usage if it produces longer responses.
[11:10] Jordan: do you have tooling to measure real token consumption per prompt?
[11:16] Maya: Console has per-request token breakdowns and the usage dashboard shows token-level cost across routes and models. we'll show the Optimize recommendations later in a follow-up.
[12:00] Carlos: now showing error scenarios: if a stream drops with 502, the SDK surfaces the last event id — you can choose to retry from last confirmed token or restart. for deterministic outputs we advise serializing the prompt state and using an idempotency key on non-streaming retries.
[12:40] Priya: what about exactly-once? we have backend side effects after generation (e.g., create ticket).
[12:48] Carlos: if you have side effects, make generation step read-only and buffer results until you commit the side effect after verifying content and dedupe via request IDs. for online pipeline, do a confirm step.
[13:35] [13:35] Alex: latency — you mentioned realistic expectations. can you give numbers?
[13:40] Carlos: depends on model and sequence length; smaller models ~50-150ms per token on our hosted infra for typical seqs, larger models higher. end-to-end chat latency with streaming and first chunk can often be 150-400ms. we can share your traffic shape and run a benchmark.
[14:05] Alex: yes we'll want to run a POC.
[14:12] Maya: noted. we'll scope it in the next meeting.
[14:30] Carlos: quick note on parameters to tune: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty, stop sequences, and logit_bias. also set a truncate policy on input tokens to avoid context overflow and unexpected costs.
[15:05] Priya: do you provide tokenizer libraries? costs vary by tokenization scheme.
[15:12] Carlos: we expose a tokenization SDK to estimate token counts client-side; SDKs have helper functions to avoid surprises.
[15:50] [15:50] Carlos: now switching to retries in code — pseudocode: try { request } catch (err) { if (err.code==429) backoffRetry(); if (5xx) limitedRetry(); else surface error } and always include an idempotency key header for non-streaming requests where you can't resume.
[16:30] Jordan: what does idempotency look like for streaming?
[16:36] Carlos: streaming resume is approximate; we provide last-event ids and short-lived resume tokens but it isn't perfect. for critical operations use non-streaming or a server-side dedupe step.
[17:10] [17:10] Carlos: showing Console -> copy as curl / copy as Node. I'll paste a sample curl in chat.
[18:00] Carlos: sample curl (non-streaming): curl -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat -H 'Authorization: Bearer $KEY' -d '{"model":"rwd-small","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize sales call"}],"max_tokens":150,"temperature":0.2}'
[18:40] Priya: can we control streaming chunk size or do you decide server-side?
[18:46] Carlos: server decides chunk boundaries but SDKs buffer to configurable chunk sizes client-side. you can tune small-chunk thresholds for UI smoothness.
[19:20] [19:20] Alex: in terms of security, how are keys rotated?
[19:25] Maya: API keys in hosted can be rotated in Console; for enterprise we offer KMS integration and short-lived tokens for automation. we'll share the security doc.
[20:05] Carlos: question on prompt injection — we recommend sanitizing user content, use system prompts with strict instructions, and apply post-generation filters. Redwood also offers built-in safety classifiers for certain plans.
[21:00] [21:00] Carlos: live tweak: switch model to 'rwd-small-v2' which is tuned for low-latency; watch the first-chunk time.
[21:30] [21:30] Alex: I can see the chunk arriving. looks good.
[22:10] Carlos: now show a retry flow — I'll force a simulated timeout on the client to emulate a network blip, SDK will attempt two retries with exponential backoff and then surface error if it fails.
[23:05] Priya: for benchmarking, what metrics should we collect?
[23:12] Carlos: collect p50/p95 latency for first byte and final token, tokens per request, error rates (4xx/5xx), retry counts, and cost per 1k tokens. also track UX metrics like perceived typing time.
[24:00] [24:00] Jordan: about billing — do you break out prompt vs completion tokens?
[24:07] Maya: yes, Console and billing show prompt vs completion token breakdown and cost.
[24:40] Carlos: final product note: Optimize can give suggestions to reduce tokens via prefix caching, batching, or recommending quantized models for Dedicated. for hosted we have intelligent suggestions in the Console's Optimize tab.
[25:30] [25:30] Alex: are there any gotchas when switching from a competitor like OpenAI?
[25:36] Carlos: differences in tokenization and response shapes; test prompts and watch for changes in length/cost. Redwood has adaptors and some migration docs.
[26:20] Priya: let's talk about support SLA — how fast to respond on incidents?
[26:25] Maya: hosted includes standard support (24-48h response), enterprise/support tiers include faster SLAs and on-call.
[27:10] [27:10] Carlos: quick Q: do you plan to use streaming for most calls or only for UI?
[27:15] Alex: UI for sure; maybe server-side for async generation on heavy loads.
[27:25] Carlos: ok good. for server-side batching you might prefer non-streaming endpoints for throughput.
[28:00] [28:00] Carlos: demo complete — recap the technical recommendations: use streaming for responsive UIs, tune temp/top_p for creativity vs determinism, use stop sequences and structured output for JSON outputs, implement exponential backoff/jitter for 429s and bounded retries for 5xx, use idempotency keys for side-effectful flows, and leverage Console/Optimize for token usage telemetry.
[29:10] Priya: any sample SLOs we should aim for?
[29:16] Carlos: for chat UIs aim p50 <200ms first chunk and p95 <500ms as a starting point for small models; we can run a POC to validate.
[30:00] [30:00] Maya: next steps — we'll send pricing and security docs, Carlos will attach sample code, and Greenline will propose POC dataset.
[30:20] Alex: sounds good. Priya will coordinate prompts.
[30:30] Priya: I'll share sample prompts later today.
[31:00] [31:00] Jordan: regarding Dedicated vs hosted — if the POC shows we need more predictable throughput, what's the timeline?
[31:10] Maya: Dedicated provisioning usually takes a few weeks depending on capacity; we'll discuss with sales if it becomes necessary.
[31:45] Carlos: one last demo note — retries and billing: if a retry is returned with an identical completion the billing will count both generation attempts; so prefer client-side dedupe when possible.
[32:20] Priya: understood. also can you include a sample of token estimator in the SDK?
[32:26] Carlos: yes will attach that.
[33:00] [33:00] Alex: any hidden limits on message size?
[33:05] Carlos: we have max context length per model; Console enforces and SDKs will truncate or reject depending on your chosen policy. we'll include exact model limits in the docs.
[34:10] [34:10] Maya: open to any final questions.
[34:16] Priya: one more — do you support webhooks for async completions?
[34:20] Carlos: yes — webhooks for async jobs are supported; they include retry semantics and signing for verification.
[35:00] [35:00] Jordan: ok we're comfortable with moving forward to POC scope.
[35:05] Maya: perfect, we'll follow up with an email that includes the items we discussed.
[35:20] Alex: thanks everyone.
[35:30] [35:30] End: quick recap in chat and link to Console recording.
